Dimos a los cristianos muchas mantas de vaca y otras cosas que traíamos; vímonos con los indios en mucho trabajo porque se volviesen a sus casas y se asegurasen y sembrasen su maíz. Ellos no querían sino ir con nosotros hasta dejarnos, como acostumbraban, con otros indios; porque si se volviesen sin hacer esto temían que se morirían; que para ir con nosotrosno temían a los cristianos ni a sus lanzas. A los cristianos les pasaba deesto, y hacían que su lengua les dijese que nosotros éramos de ellos mismos, y nos habíamos perdidomuchos tiempos había, y que éramos gente de poca suerte y valor, y que ellos eran los señores de aquella tierra, a quien habían de obedecer y servir. Mas todo esto los indios tenían en muy poco o en nada de lo que les decían; anntes, unos con otros sí platicaban, diciendo que los cristianos mentían porque nosotros veníamos de donde salía el sol, y ellos donde se pone; y que nosotros sanábamos los enfermos, y ellos mataban los que estaban sanos; y que nosotros veníamos desnudos y descalzos, y ellos vestidos y en caballos con lanzas; y que nosotros no teníamos cobdicia de ninguna cosa, antes todo cuanto nos daban torntábamos luego a dar, y con nada nos quedábamos y los otros no tenían otro fin sino robar todo cuanto hallaban, y nunca daban nada nadie; y de esta manera relataban todas nuestras cosas y las encarescían, por el contrario, de los otros; y así les respondieron a la lengua de los cristianos, y lo mismo hicieron saber a los otros por una lengua que ellos había, con quien entendíamos, y aquellos que la usan llamamos propriamente primahaitu, que es como decir vascongados, la cual, más de cuatrocientas leguas de las que anduvimos, hallamos usada entre ellos, sin haber otra por todas aquellas tierras. Finalmente, nunca pudo acabar con los indicios creer que éramos de los otros cristianos, y con mucho trabajo e importunación les hecimos volvera su casa, y les mandamos que se asegurasen, y asentasen sus pueblos, y sembrasen y labrasen la tierra, que, de estar despoblada, estaba ya muy llenade montes; la cual sin dubda es la mejor de cuantas en estas Indias hay, y más fértil y abundosa de mantenimientos, y siembran tres veces en el año. Tienen muchas frutas y muy hermosos ríos, y otras muchas aguas muy buenas. Hay muestras grandes y señales de minas de oro y plata; la gente de ella es muy bien acondicionada; sirven a los cristianos (los que son amigos) de muy buena voluntad. Son muy dispuestos, mucho más que los de Méjico, y, finalmente, estierra que ninguna cosa le falta para ser muy buena. Despedidos los indios, nos dijeron que harían lo que mandábamos, y asentarían sus pueblos si los cristianos los dejaban; y yo así lo digo y afirmo pormuy cierto, que si no lo hicieren será por culpa de los cristianos. Después que hobimos enviado a los indios en paz, y degraciadoles el trabajo que con nosotros habían pasado, los cristianos nos enviaron, debajo de cautela, a un Cebreros, alcalde, y con él otros dos, los cuales nos llevaron por los montes y despoblados, por apartarnos de la conversación de los indios, y porque no viésemos ni entendiésemos lo que de hecho hicieron; donde paresce cuánto se engañan los pensamientos de los hombres, que nosotros andabamosa les buscar libertad, y cuando pensábamos que la teníamos, sucedió tal al contrario, porque tenían acordado de ir a dar en los indios que enviábamos asegurados y de paz; y ansí como lo pensaron, lo hicieron; lleváronnos por aquellos montes dos días, sin agua, perdidos y sin camino, y todos pensamos perecer de sed, y de ella se nos ahogaron siete hombres, y muchos amigos que los cristianos traían consigo no pudieron llegar hasta otro día a mediodíaadonde aquella noche hallamos con ellos veinte y cinco leguas, poco más o menos, y al fin de ellas llegamos a un pueblo de indios de paz, y el alcalde que nos llevaba nos dejó allí, y él pasó adelante otras tres leguas, a un pueblo que se llamaba Culiazan, adonde estaba Melchor Díaz, alcalde mayor y capitán de aquella provincia.

### CAPITULO XXXV

*De cómo el alcalde mayor nos recibió bien la noche que llegamos*

Como el alcalde mayor fue avisado de nuestra salida y venida, luego aquella noche partió, y vino adonde nosotros estábamos, y lloró mucho con nosotros, dando loores a Dios nuestro Señor por haber usado de tanta misericordia con nosotros; y nos habló y trato muy bien; y de parte del gobernador Nuño de Guzman y suya nos ofreció todo lo que tenía y podía; y mostró mucho sentimiento de la mala acogida y tratamiento que en Alcaraz y los otros habíamos hallado, y tuvimos por cierto que si el se hallara allí, se excusara lo que con nosotros y con los indios se hizo; y pasada aquella noche, otro día nos partimos, y el alcalde mayor nos rogó mucho que nos detuviésemos allí, y que en esto haríamos muy gran servicio a Dios y a Vuestra Majestad, porque la tierra estaba despoblada, sin labrarse, y toda muy destruida, y los indios andaban es-

That night we gave thanks to God our Lord for bringing us out of our captivity,</meta> except for the food, and we gave everything else to the Christians so they could divide it among themselves. After this, we had many great disputes with them because they did not want to set free the Indians we were bringing as slaves. Because of this anger, upon departing, we left behind many Turkish-style bows that we were carrying, as well as many pouches and arrows. Among them were the five emeralds, which we completely forgot about, and thus we lost them. We gave the Christians many cow hides <note>likely bison hides</note> and other things we were carrying. We saw ourselves in great difficulty with the Indians to get them to return to their homes, reassure themselves, and plant their corn. They did not want anything but to go with us until they could leave us, as they were accustomed, with other Indians; for if they returned without doing this, they feared they would die. To go with us, they did not fear the Christians or their lances.

The Christians cared little about this and made their <term>lengua</term> <gloss>interpreter</gloss> tell them that we were of their own kind, that we had been lost a long time ago, that we were people of little luck and value, and that they were the lords of that land whom they had to obey and serve. But the Indians valued all of this very little or not at all. Instead, they spoke among themselves, saying that the Christians were lying because we came from where the sun rises and they from where it sets; that we healed the sick and they killed those who were healthy; that we came naked and barefoot, and they were clothed and on horses with lances; that we felt no greed for anything, but rather gave away everything we were given, never keeping anything for ourselves, while the others had no goal other than to steal everything they found and never gave anything to anyone. In this way, they recounted all our deeds and praised them, in contrast to the others. 

They responded this way to the Christians' interpreter, and they made the same known to others through an interpreter they had, whom we could understand. Those who use that language we call properly <term>primahaitu</term> <gloss>a term Cabeza de Vaca uses to describe a widely understood common language, comparing it to Basque</gloss>, which is like saying "Basque speakers." We found it used among them for more than four hundred leagues of what we traveled, without finding any other throughout those lands. Finally, we could never convince the Indians to believe that we were of the other Christians, and with much labor and insistence, we made them return to their homes. We ordered them to be reassured, settle their villages, and plant and till the land, which, due to being depopulated, was already very full of thickets. It is without a doubt the best of all that there are in these Indies, the most fertile and abundant in provisions, and they plant three times a year. They have many fruits and very beautiful rivers, and many other very good waters. There are great signs and traces of gold and silver mines. The people of it are very well-disposed; they serve the Christians (those who are friends) with very good will. They are very capable, much more so than those of Mexico, and, finally, it is a land that lacks nothing to be very good. 

Once the Indians had left, they told us they would do what we ordered and would settle their villages if the Christians let them. I say and affirm this as very certain: if they do not do so, it will be the fault of the Christians. After we had sent the Indians away in peace and thanked them for the effort they had undergone with us, the Christians sent us, under guard, to a certain Cebreros, an <term>alcalde</term> <gloss>magistrate/mayor</gloss>, and with him two others. They took us through the mountains and uninhabited lands to distance us from the company of the Indians, and so that we would not see or understand what they actually did. It appears here how deceived the thoughts of men are: we were walking to seek their freedom, and when we thought we had obtained it, the exact opposite happened, because they had planned to go and attack the Indians whom we had sent back reassured and in peace. And just as they planned it, they did it. They led us through those mountains for two days without water, lost and without a path, and we all thought we would perish from thirst. Seven men died from it, and many friends the Christians were bringing with them could not arrive until the next day at midday where we had been with them that night, twenty-five leagues, more or less. At the end of that, we arrived at a town of peaceful Indians, and the magistrate who was leading us left us there, and he went on three leagues further to a town called Culiazan, where Melchor Díaz, the <term>alcalde mayor</term> <gloss>chief magistrate</gloss> and captain of that province, was.

### CAPITULO XXXV

*Of how the chief magistrate received us well the night we arrived*

As the chief magistrate was informed of our departure and arrival, he left that same night and came to where we were. He wept a great deal with us, giving praise to God our Lord for having used so much mercy with us. He spoke to us and treated us very well; and on behalf of Governor Nuño de Guzman and himself, he offered us everything he had and could. He showed great regret for the bad reception and treatment we had encountered in Alcaraz and the others, and we held it for certain that if he had been there, what was done to us and to the Indians would have been avoided. Once that night had passed, the next day we departed, and the chief magistrate begged us a great deal to stay there, and that in doing so we would do a great service to God and to Your Majesty, because the land was depopulated, not being farmed, and all very destroyed, and the Indians were wandering...

<summary>Cabeza de Vaca describes his struggle to protect the indigenous people from the deceitful treatment of fellow Christians, noting the contrast between his group’s peaceful conduct and the Spanish soldiers' greed. Despite his efforts, he is placed under guard by officials, only to be later received with kindness by the chief magistrate, Melchor Díaz.</summary>

He possesses a **distinctive appearance** <note>original: "svasvarūpaḥ"; implies a form that is characteristic or true to his own nature</note>. He has **prominent cheekbones**, a **high nose**, and a **round forehead**. He is **full of desire** <note>original: "kāmābhilāṣī"; referring to a sensual or passionate temperament</note>. He is **prosperous**, with wealth that seems to gather in the "lotus-base" of his face <note>original: "mukhe kamalatale vadhadhanaḥ"; an idiomatic way of saying his prosperity is evident in his countenance or speech</note>.

His constitution is governed by the **Vata and Kapha humors** <term>vata-śleshma</term> <note>the biological energies of "wind" and "phlegm" in Ayurvedic medicine, often resulting in a frame that is either very lean or prone to steadiness and cool temperament</note>. He is **inclined toward laziness**. He is a **devotee of his teacher, the gods, and the sacred fire**.

He is **fair-complexioned** and **resolute** in nature. At the time of birth, he is as small as a **Raktika seed** <note>original: "rattikā samāḥ"; the Raktika or Gunja seed was a traditional unit of weight; this likely refers to a specific physical measurement or a birthmark</note>. He has **prominent veins** <note>original: "vāyavī-śirāḥ"; literally "wind-veins," a physical trait often associated with the Vata constitution</note> and is **endowed with auspicious lines on the soles of his feet**. He is **fond of royal assemblies** <note>original: "rājasabhā-priyaḥ"; suggests he enjoys the company of high society or political circles</note>. He is one who **subsists on milk** <note>original: "kṣīrabhojī"; implies a refined, pure, or "Sattvic" diet</note>, and he is **exceptionally fortunate**.

The Commentary on the Images states: "The good fortune of the six-five line brings celebration."

Celebration means joy. However, the fifth line occupies the ruler's position, and what it accumulates is great; therefore, it is called celebration. This refers to the ancient saying: "When the sovereign possesses virtue, the realm rejoices."

Nine at the top: Carrying the highway of heaven, success.

This expresses the principle that accumulation reaches its extremity and dissolves into free passage. <term>He</term> <gloss>carrying</gloss> is pronounced as <term>he</term> <note>glossed here phonetically by the fanqie spelling hu-ke</note>, meaning to carry on the shoulder or bear on the back. <term>Dan</term> <gloss>to bear</gloss> is the same as the character <term>dan</term> <gloss>carrying pole / burden</gloss>, as in Yang Xiong's phrase <term>dan shi</term> <gloss>a peck and a stone of grain</gloss>. In the Book of Songs, the phrases "carrying a rain cloak" and "wearing a bamboo hat" both pronounce <term>he</term> in this tone. The Rhapsody on the Hall of Lingguang states: "Carrying the highway of heaven to attain primal success." Zhuangzi's phrase "bearing the blue sky upon one's back" shares this exact meaning. Zheng Kangcheng also explained that it means carrying upon the shoulder. The single yang line at the very top resembles a carrying pole, while the two yin lines hanging down on either side resemble loads suspended on both ends. This forms the visual image of carrying a shoulder pole. It signifies a single shoulder pole lifting up the grand highway of heaven. This is precisely what Chen Baisha meant when he wrote of making the bright moon and cool breeze into two loads suspended from a pole.

CHAPTER XI.

## Armenia.

Armenia itself—that is, in Lajazzo <note>modern Ayas or Yumurtalık, Turkey; a major port of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia</note>—is where the bulk of the merchandise is traded, because it is on the coast and merchant residents live there continually.

Pepper, ginger, sugar, cinnamon, incense, brazilwood <note>original: "verzino," a wood used to produce red dye</note>, lacquer, cotton, and all bulk spices, as well as iron, copper, and tin, are all sold in Armenia by the *ruotolo* <note>a standard Mediterranean unit of weight, the rotolo</note> of 15 *occhia* <note>the okka, a common unit of weight in the Eastern Mediterranean, roughly 1.2 kg</note> per *ruotolo*, and 33 *ruotoli* make one *Catars* <note>a cantaro or hundredweight</note> of Armenia.

Silk and all fine spices are sold there by the *occhia* at a rate of 12 *occhia* per *ruotolo*, and this is called the "market *occhia*."

Gold is sold by weight, where 50 *pesi* <term>pesi: literally "weights"</term> make 1 *mars* <note>a mark, a unit of weight for precious metals</note> of Armenia.

Silver is sold by the *mars*, which is 50 *pesi*.

Hides are sold by the weight of the mark, and 40 of these weights are given for one large *ara* <note>a specific measurement or bundle size</note> of hide.

Linen cloths and canvases are sold by the hundred *canne* <term>canna</term> <note>a "cane" or rod, a linear measure of roughly 2 meters</note>, at the price of a certain number of Bezants <note>original: "Bisanti," a gold or silver coin used throughout the Levant</note>, with 10 *taccolini* <note>likely the Armenian takvorin, a silver coin</note> per Bezant.

Soap, wool, and camlets <note>original: "ciambellotti," a cloth made from camel or goat hair</note> are sold by the *ruotolo* of 15 *occhia*.

Grain is sold at Lajazzo in Armenia by the *moggio* <note>a dry measure for grain</note> and by the *marzapanni*; that is, in bulk by the *moggio* and in smaller amounts by the *marzapanni*, and 10 *marzapanni* make 1 *moggio*.

Crimson silk is sold by the *occhia*, which weighs 110 *diremo* <note>the dirhem, a small unit of weight used for high-value goods</note>.

Saffron is sold by the *occhia*, which weighs 112 *diremo*.

Oil is sold by the barrel, just as it is.

The Bezant of Romania <note>referring to the Latin Empire or Byzantine territories</note> is counted as 10 silver *taccolini*, and the *taccolino* is worth 10 Armenian *denari* <note>pennies</note>, and the *denaro* is worth 4 *folleri* <note>small copper coins</note>.

->*What the Armenian Mint gives for a mark of silver to whoever brings it to the said Mint:*<-

Of Sardinian silver - - - - - - - - - - - 114 *taccolini*, 1 *denaro*.
Of Venetian bullion plates <note>original: "piatte della bolla di Vinegia"</note> - 113 *taccolini* and 1 *denaro*.
At the alloy of the *Gros tournois* <note>original: "Tornesi grossi," a silver coin of France</note> - 111 *taccolini*.
At the alloy of the *Gigliati* <note>original: "Gigliati," silver coins of Naples/Provence featuring lilies</note> - 110 *taccolini* and 5 *denari*.
Of bracelets, that is, *Buenmini* <note>likely referring to Bohemian groschen or a specific form of imported bullion</note> - 109 *taccolini* and 2 *denari*.

<margin>things that kill the embryo</margin>

**T**here are things that harm the embryo and not the mother, and conversely, and some harm both. Whence, wishing to establish a foundation, we say that the herb poppy and its seed harm both. The cause is that they induce sleep in both, and the herb stains the skin of the embryo with a spot that never departs. It should be known that the poppy and the white rose make a white spot, and the red one, a red spot. Whence a pregnant woman should not use them in food, lest the child become sleepy or spotted. The meat of the hare and the lion harms the embryo greatly because the former sleeps with its eyes open, and the latter similarly. Vinegar harms it, and suet, that is, the nerves of the feet of oxen, and milk and cucumber, in that they induce excessive coldness. Whence they carry danger to both. Lily and saffron harm the embryo and stain its skin a pale color. Leek, garlic, lettuce, and dill harm the embryo in that they deprive it of sight. Adel and alleum, that is, a large root in the bark, harm the embryo in that they corrupt the connection of the fingers of the hand, etc. The teeth grow late, and they are quickly deprived. Basil, wormwood, salt, and pepper harm the embryo in that through them it will be dry in flesh and becomes leprous from excessive heat, and it will have short nails. Pure cumin harms it on account of epilepsy. The meat of the pig and the eel harms it on account of the grime in the marrow of the bones and the dirt in the mouth. Salted meat, rustic cheese, and fried food harm it in that through them it becomes dry in flesh. And glutten, hyssop, caruca, dried figs, pine nuts, and morsels in wine, if not taken in excess, help the embryo and the womb, because they render it fat and bring color to the face. Sage, mint, fennel, and parsley are valuable to both because they generate good wind. Savory, pennyroyal, and borage kill the embryo. The smoke of an extinguished candle and lantern, the subtle steam of sulfur, and silver kill the embryo and harm the brain of the woman. When indeed the embryo moves, having hair, it causes pain to the woman in the belly or prickings. Also, it is to be known that the end of all humors in quantity, as much in time as in the person, when they are combined, becomes a sensory perception, as Galen says in his <term>Microtegni</term> <gloss>Small Art (of Medicine)</gloss>.
